description: Calculate the real Pearson correlation between two assets (BTC, NASDAQ, S&P 500) by pasting their return series. Get the coefficient from -1 to +1 instantly, free.
intro: This calculator measures the **real correlation** between two assets — for example **BTC and the NASDAQ**, or **BTC and the S&P 500** — from the data you paste in. You enter two lists of numbers (daily/monthly returns or closing prices) separated by commas and it returns the **Pearson correlation coefficient**, which ranges from **-1 to +1**: +1 means they move identically, 0 means no relationship, -1 means they move in opposite directions. It uses **no pre-loaded values** — the result comes entirely from the series you enter.
keyTakeaway: Paste two series with the same number of values to get the **Pearson r** between them. |r| ≥ 0.6 = strong correlation (little diversification); 0.3–0.6 = moderate; < 0.3 = weak (good diversification). The sign shows whether they move together (+) or in opposite directions (−). For reference only, not financial advice.

explanation:
Bitcoin spent its first decade marketed as "digital gold" — an asset decoupled from traditional markets. That thesis weakened after 2020: with institutional adoption, spot ETFs, and BTC desks at major banks, it increasingly trades like a risk-on asset alongside tech stocks. Measuring how two assets actually move together stops being academic when it drives portfolio decisions.

This calculator uses **no pre-loaded values**: you paste the two series of returns (or prices) yourself, and it computes the real Pearson correlation coefficient between them so you can see, with your own numbers, how tightly they are linked.

## How Correlation Is Calculated

The calculator applies the Pearson correlation coefficient to the two vectors you enter:

```
r(X,Y) = Σ (xᵢ - x̄)(yᵢ - ȳ) / √[ Σ(xᵢ - x̄)² · Σ(yᵢ - ȳ)² ]

where:
  X = asset A series (e.g. BTC returns)
  Y = asset B series (e.g. NASDAQ returns)
  x̄, ȳ = means of each series
  r ∈ [-1, +1]
```

Both series must have the **same number of values** and at least 3 data points. You can use daily returns, monthly returns, or closing prices — what matters is that position i in series A lines up with the same period as position i in series B.

## Correlation Levels and Their Meaning

| r range | Reading | Portfolio implication |
|---|---|---|
| -1.0 to -0.7 | Strong negative | Move in opposite directions; useful as a hedge |
| -0.7 to -0.3 | Moderate negative | Partial hedge |
| -0.3 to +0.3 | Low / none | Effective diversification; independent risk |
| +0.3 to +0.6 | Moderate | Partial diversification; tend to move together in crises |
| +0.6 to +0.85 | High | Very similar behavior; little diversification |
| +0.85 to +1.0 | Very high | Statistically almost the same asset |

## Things to Keep in Mind

- **Use returns, not raw prices** when possible — price correlation is inflated by trend.
- **Correlation isn't causation**: BTC and the NASDAQ moving together may reflect a common factor (market risk appetite), not one driving the other.
- **Short series are unstable**: under ~30 observations the coefficient can be misleading, even though the calc accepts from 3.
- **Pearson captures only linear association**: a curved relationship can show r≈0 yet still be related.

## Final Notes

This calculation is a reference tool only. Correlation is historical and does not predict the future — in systemic crises most risk assets fall together. For critical financial decisions, consult a licensed financial advisor.

faq.q: What do I need to enter?
faq.a: Two series of comma-separated numbers: series A (e.g. BTC returns) and series B (e.g. NASDAQ returns). Both must have the same number of values and at least 3 data points each.

faq.q: What is the Pearson correlation coefficient?
faq.a: A statistical measure from -1 to +1. +1 means the two series move identically, 0 means no linear relationship, -1 means they move in exactly opposite directions. The calculator computes it from your data — no pre-loaded values.

faq.q: How do I interpret the result?
faq.a: By magnitude (|r|): ≥ 0.6 is strong, 0.3–0.6 moderate, below 0.3 weak. The sign gives direction: positive = they move together, negative = they move in opposite directions.

faq.q: Does it only work for BTC, NASDAQ and S&P 500?
faq.a: No. It works for any pair of numeric series: two cryptos, a stock and an index, gold vs bonds, etc. The name reflects the most-searched case, but the formula is generic.

faq.q: Should I use prices or returns?
faq.a: Returns (period-over-period percentage change) are recommended, because price correlation is usually inflated by the trend. The calc accepts any series of numbers you paste.

faq.q: Does high correlation mean one asset causes the other's moves?
faq.a: No. Correlation does not imply causation. BTC and the NASDAQ moving together may be driven by a common factor (market risk appetite) rather than one causing the other.

faq.q: How many data points do I need for a reliable result?
faq.a: The calc requires a minimum of 3 pairs, but below ~30 observations the coefficient is unstable. For serious analysis use at least 30–90 periods.

faq.q: Why is Bitcoin correlated with NASDAQ?
faq.a: Since 2020 BTC trades as a risk-on asset: it rises with tech stocks when markets have risk appetite and falls with them during risk-off. That's why it adds little diversification to a stock portfolio when correlation is high.

For diversification, yes: an asset negatively correlated with your portfolio tends to rise when the rest falls, acting as a hedge. But correlations change, especially in crises when almost everything falls together.
